  %\VignetteIndexEntry{Instrumental-variable models}
  %\VignetteEngine{knitr::rmarkdown}

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
site <- identical(Sys.getenv("IN_PKGDOWN"), "true")
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", eval = site,
                      message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
options(width = 100)
```

Two-stage least squares models fit with `fixest::feols()` can be combined
like any other model. Here median rent in the 50 states (1980 Census) is
regressed on median housing value, treated as endogenous, and the percent of
the population that is urban. The first model instruments housing value with
family income; the second adds the census regions as instruments.

```{r iv}
library(suest)
library(marginaleffects)
library(haven)
library(fixest)

hsng <- zap_labels(read_dta("https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/hsng2.dta"))

iv1 <- feols(rent ~ pcturban | hsngval ~ faminc, data = hsng)
iv2 <- feols(rent ~ pcturban | hsngval ~ faminc + factor(region), data = hsng)
fit_iv <- suest(iv1, iv2, model_names = c("Income", "Income and region"))
fit_iv
```

The effect of percent urban in each model, and the difference:

```{r iv-effects}
urban <- avg_slopes(fit_iv, variables = "pcturban", newdata = hsng)
urban
hypotheses(urban, hypothesis = difference ~ revpairwise)
```

**Example interpretation:** Neither model shows a significant effect of the
percent urban on rent. But the effects differ significantly across the two
sets of instruments: adding the regions as instruments raises the effect by
0.59 (\(p < .05\)).
